title: Killing a Vortex
authors: Dimitrios M. Thilikos (LIRMM, Univ. de Montpellier, CNRS, France), Sebastian Wiederrecht (LIRMM, Univ. de Montpellier, CNRS and DIMAG, IBS, South Korea)
abstract: We provide a "vortex-free" refinement of the seminal structure theorem for K_t-minor free graphs by Robertson and Seymour as follows: we identify a (parameterized) graph H_t and prove that if we replace K_t by H_t, then the resulting decomposition becomes "vortex-free". Up to now, the most general classes of graphs admitting such a result were either bounded Euler genus graphs or the single-crossing minor-free graphs. This result is tight in the sense that whenever we minor-exclude a graph that is not a minor of some H_t, the appearance of vortices is unavoidable. Using the above decomposition theorem, we design an algorithm that, given an H_t-minor-free graph G, computes the generating function of all perfect matchings of G in polynomial time. This algorithm yields, on H_t-minor-free graphs, polynomial algorithms for computational problems such as the {dimer problem, the exact matching problem}, and the computation of the permanent. Our results, combined with known complexity results, imply a complete characterization of minor-closed graph classes where the number of perfect matchings is polynomially computable: They are precisely those graph classes that do not contain every H_t as a minor. This provides a sharp complexity dichotomy for the problem of counting perfect matchings in minor-closed classes.

Abstract—We provide a “vortex-free” reﬁnement of the seminal structure theorem for Kt -minor free graphs by Robertson
and Seymour as follows: we identify a (parameterized) graph
Ht and we prove that if we replace Kt by Ht , then the
resulting decomposition becomes “vortex-free”. Up to now, the
most general classes of graphs admitting such a result were either
bounded Euler genus graphs or the single-crossing minor-free
graphs. This result is tight in the sense that, whenever we minorexclude a graph that is not a minor of some Ht , the appearance of
vortices is unavoidable. Using the above decomposition theorem,
we design an algorithm that, given an Ht -minor-free graph G,
computes the generating function of all perfect matchings of G in
polynomial time. This algorithm yields, on Ht -minor-free graphs,
polynomial algorithms for computational problems such as the
dimer problem, the exact matching problem, and the computation
of the permanent. Our results, combined with known complexity
results, imply a complete characterization of minor-closed graph
classes where the number of perfect matchings is polynomially
computable: They are precisely those graph classes that do not
contain every Ht as a minor. This provides a sharp complexity
dichotomy for the problem of counting perfect matchings in
minor-closed classes.
Index Terms—Perfect Matchings, Permanent, Pfafﬁan Orientations, Graph Minors, Counting Algorithms, Graph Parameters.

B. Counting matchings in minor-closed graph classes
In what concerns general (i.e., non-bipartite) graphs,
Kasteleyn claimed in [18], [19] that his algorithm for
#P ERFECT M ATCHING on planar graphs can be extended to
graphs of bounded Euler genus. This was proven by Galluccio
and Loebl [10] for orientable surfaces and by Tesler [38] for
non-orientable surfaces. The later results were based on a reduction of the problem to the computation of 2g orientations3 ,
where g is the Euler genus of the input graph. A uniﬁed
algorithm for counting the number of perfect matchings on
graphs of bounded Euler genus without the use of orientations
was given by Curticapean and Xia in [5].
Notice that graphs of bounded Euler genus are minor-closed.
The emerging question is whether #P ERFECT M ATCHING is
polynomially solvable for all minor-closed graph classes. For

#P ERFECT M ATCHING(F) for the #P ERFECT M ATCHING
problem restricted to graphs excluding all graphs in F
as minors. We stress that every minor-closed graph class

Let Γ be the cross-free drawing of some (planar) graph G on
a disk Δ. The face of Γ whose closure contains the boundary
of Δ is called external face of Γ. Let Q be the set of vertices
of G that are incident to this (unique) external face.
The ring blowup of Γ is the graph G obtained from G by
introducing for each u ∈ Q a new vertex vu together with
the edge uvu , the edges {wvu | w ∈ NG (u)}, and the edges
{vu vw | w ∈ NG (u) ∩ Q}. A graph G is called a ring blowup
graph if it is a subgraph of some graph isomorphic to the ring
blowup of a cross-free drawing on a disk Δ of some planar
graph. For instance K7 is the ring blowup of any cross-free
drawing of K4 on a disk Δ (see Figure 7 for another example).
Proposition 5 ([7]): Counting perfect matchings is #P-hard
on the class of ring blowup graphs.
